amendments.rule: The conjunction `וְ` is normally English *and*, including the waw of a consecutive verb form: the conjunction takes *And* and the verb takes the verb. Where the ASV renders it by some other connective, align it to that word instead. **The list is open and is read off the ASV rather than checked against a set**: the corpus already aligns a waw to *but*, *then*, *so*, *or*, *now*, *also*, *for*, *therefore*, *neither*, *nor*, *yea*, *yet*, *even*, *with*, *moreover* and *howbeit*, among others. A connective the ASV has written for a waw is never `added`, and it is never folded into a neighbouring word to avoid one: a town list writes *with* for the waw of `וְחַצְרֵיהֶן` → *with their villages* and *even* for the waw of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea*, and each waw takes the word written for it. **Where the ASV renders one connective morpheme by a correlative pair such as *both … and*, *either … or* or *whether … or*, both English words belong to that morpheme's one discontinuous unit, headed on the closing connective (*and* or *or*); the opening correlative is not `added`.** **This governs the disjunctive `אוֹ` exactly as it governs a waw**, since what licenses the pair is the one connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma: `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` → ***whether*** *a male* ***or*** *a female* gives *whether … or* to the single `אוֹ`, headed on *or*. Where the Hebrew instead writes a connective of its own for each member — `אוֹ … אוֹ` → *either … or* — each takes only the English word written for it and there is no pair to place. **But that governs only a pair no other morpheme has a claim on.** Where another morpheme standing in the clause is itself what the opening correlative says — a present negative for the *neither* of *neither … nor*, the `מִן` of a `מִן … עַד` range for the *both* of *both … and* — that morpheme takes the opening word and the waw takes only the closing connective, exactly as rule 47 gives a written *the* to a present article before a supplied one and rule 46 gives a *that* to a present relative before a bare participle. `אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ הֵמָּה וַאֲבוֹתָם` → *whom* ***neither*** *they* ***nor*** *their fathers have known* gives *neither* to `לֹא` and *nor* to the waw, and `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` → ***both*** *the birds of the heavens* ***and*** *the beasts* gives *both* to `מִן` and *and* to the waw, leaving the `עַד` `unrepresented` under rule 40. **A morpheme that merely stands where the opening correlative stands has no claim on it.** What gives another morpheme that word is that the morpheme is itself what the correlative says, so read sense and not position: the two `לְ`s of `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` stand exactly where an English *whether* and a second *for* would stand, and a benefactive preposition is not what *whether* says, so both are `unrepresented` under rule 40 and neither takes the word. Count the correlative's members against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. This does not touch rule 35's fusion, which is a single English word carrying every morpheme's sense: a lone *Nor* or *neither* with no answering *nor* written is that rule's, and only a written pair is this one's. Read what stands in the clause for that waw in particular, as rule 51 requires for *also*, and where the ASV leaves it unrendered, mark it `unrepresented`. **But read whether a waw is present at all before placing the connective.** Where the ASV writes a coordinating *and*, *or* or *but* for a clause or phrase in which no conjunction morpheme stands, no morpheme licenses that word and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30. Hebrew juxtaposes where English coordinates, and the ASV supplies the connective freely: `עַל־כָּתֵף תִּשָּׂא בָּעֲלָטָה תוֹצִיא` → *shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulder,* ***and*** *carry it forth in the dark* writes one for a clause the Hebrew leaves asyndetic, and `לְיוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם אֶל־אַדְמַת יִשְׂרָאֵל` → *concerning the inhabitants of Jerusalem* ***and*** *the land of Israel* writes one for a second prepositional phrase the Hebrew merely sets beside the first. Do not fold such a word into the preposition, the verb or the noun standing next to it to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them, and a preposition whose own relation the ASV has left unstated is `unrepresented` under rule 40 rather than a home for a coordinator. Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's connectives, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. Read the clause before counting, since a morpheme that has an English word of its own is not made a surplus by this sentence: a present negative carries a *nor* or a *neither* under rule 35, a `כִּי` or an `אִם` carries a *but* or an *or* the ASV has written for it, and only a connective no morpheme answers to is `added`. **And a coordinator standing inside one morpheme's own English rendering is not a connective supplied for the clause at all.** Where the ASV renders a single source morpheme by a fixed English phrase that contains an *and* or an *or*, the word coordinates the parts of that phrase and not two source items, so it belongs to that morpheme's unit, is neither `added` nor a separate connective, and does not move the unit's head, which rule 44 leaves on the lexical verb because a phrasal particle names nothing on its own. Decide it by asking what stands on either side of the English word in the Hebrew, which is the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use and the one rule 30 applies to its one-English-word condition. Where a source clause or phrase stands on each side, the preceding sentences govern and a connective no waw answers to is `added`; where the same one morpheme's rendering runs on both sides and no source item is coordinated at all, the word is written inside that rendering rather than beside it. `וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתוֹךְ אֲרָיוֹת` → *And he went up and down among the lions* keeps *up and down* whole with the one verb it renders, while `אָבְדָה תִקְוָתָהּ` → ***and*** *her hope was lost* leaves its supplied *and* `added`, because there a written clause stands on either side of it.
amendments.why: LEV.12.7 met the case rule 14's correlative sentence had not considered: the ASV renders a single `אוֹ` by *whether … or*, and the rule spoke only of a waw, so a reader had either to reason by analogy or to place *whether* somewhere else. The chapter shows the trap the rule leaves open — the earlier alignment gave *whether* to the `לְ` of `לַזָּכָר` on the ground that it stands in that slot, and BSB likewise represents both `לְ`s — so the amendment states what the existing limit implies but never says: the claim is on sense, not position, and a benefactive preposition is not what *whether* says. Nothing in the corpus contradicts it. `אוֹ` is aligned to *or* in 133 units, to *either* in 5 and to *whether* in 5, every one of those being a member of a written `אוֹ … אוֹ` pair where each particle takes the word standing with it, which is exactly what the added closing sentence preserves; no corpus unit places a correlative on a preposition. The rest of rule 14, including the `מִן … עַד` and `neither … nor` limits, the open-list sentence, the absent-waw count and the phrase-internal coordinator clause, is reproduced unchanged.

conventions: The purification formula appears in two shapes in this chapter and MACULA's morphology, not the English, decides the italic *her*: `דְּמֵי טָהֳרָה` at 12.4 and 12.5 has an absolute `טָהֳרָה` (Ncbsa) with no suffix on it, so the ASV's italic *her* before *purifying* answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit under rule 18's closing sentence, while `יְמֵי טָהֳרָהּ` at 12.4 and 12.6 carries a suffix that takes the written *her* under rule 18. The two phrases are rendered by the same English words, so read the tag before placing the possessive; the italic corroborates and decides nothing, by rule 7.

Three construct chains here turn on whether the construct noun keeps an English word of its own, and rule 19 divides them two ways: `בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ` → *a year old* gives *old* to `בֶּן` and *a year* to the rectum (12.6), and `דֵּי שֶׂה` → *for a lamb* gives *for* to `דֵּי` and *a lamb* to the rectum (12.8), because in each the construct would otherwise be left holding nothing; but `תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת` → *the law for her that beareth* (12.7) leaves *law* on the construct, so the relational *for* is the rectum's and goes to the participle carrying the lexeme, discontinuous around the substantival article's *her that*, exactly as `of … purifying` runs around the suffix's *her* at 12.4 and 12.6. Count the ASV's words against the two nouns before placing a preposition in the parallel purification and offering laws.

report: All 26 candidate lemma groups were read. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed either by the ASV's own wording (וְ → And/and/But/then by clause position; אֶל → into the sanctuary vs unto the priest/door; כִּפֶּר with and without its auxiliary; מָלֵא → be fulfilled after עַד vs are fulfilled after temporal בְּ; אֶחָד → the one / the other) or by a difference in the source itself (הוּא Sp3ms: an object suffix rendered it at 12.7 against an unwritten possessive in בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ at 12.6; הַ: a written the at 12.3/12.4/12.6/12.8 against ASV's indefinite a male / a female at 12.7). None is a split.

The table is blind to `added` units, so the dump was read end to end for the reverse case — a supplied word folded in one verse and marked `added` in another. The chapter has exactly two `added` units, the italic her at 12.4 t009 and 12.5 t027, and both rest on the same morphological fact: דְּמֵי טָהֳרָה carries an absolute Ncbsa with no suffix, while יְמֵי טָהֳרָהּ at 12.4 and 12.6 carries a suffix that takes the written her. Nowhere does the chapter fold a supplied possessive into a noun. Recorded as a convention.

Construct division is consistent across the three chains where a preposition or attributive was in question: בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ → old on the construct (12.6) and דֵּי שֶׂה → for on the construct (12.8), both under rule 19's rider because the construct would otherwise hold nothing, against תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת → law on the construct and the relational for on the rectum (12.7) under rule 19's first sentence. The same subtraction decided all three. Recorded as a convention.

Rule 31's supplied generics are uniform: burnt offering and sin offering head on burnt/sin in all four units, man child and maid child head on man/maid, hallowed thing heads on hallowed, and both turtle dove units (12.6, 12.8) head on dove/doves under the tie clause with the competing head named in each note. Rule 22's tail-to-tail יוֹם and rule 42's waw/and count are applied identically at 12.4 and 12.5.

BSB: all 8 disagreements are documented convention differences, and none is a genuine error. לֵאמֹר's לְ (12.1) is rule 27 verbatim; the two יוֹם (12.4, 12.5) are the tail-to-tail case rule 22 names BSB as disagreeing on; the ordinal's agreement article (12.3) is rule 47; בְּכָל־קֹדֶשׁ's בְּ (12.4) is rule 40's promoted object (touch no hallowed thing writes nothing for it); בֶּן־שְׁנָתוֹ's suffix (12.6) has no possessive in a year old; and the two לַ of 12.7 have no English because the ASV writes whether a male or a female where BSB writes to a male. No accepted edge was moved to improve the rate.

The chapter's one live inconsistency was already resolved inside the verse pass at 12.7, which moved whether off the first לְ onto the אוֹ that now carries the discontinuous whether … or headed on or, leaving both לְ unrepresented. That reading is left as accepted and is promoted as an amendment to rule 14, which had stated the correlative-pair rule for the waw alone and left the positional temptation unaddressed.
